title: One Side or Both S. Korea Rethinks Escalator Rules
paragraphs: How should people ride an escalator? Should they stand on one side and leave the other side free for people who want to walk, or should they stand on both sides? In South Korea, this simple question has become a surprisingly big debate.

In August 2026, South Korea's Interior Ministry surveyed 1,000 adults in seven major cities. The results showed that the country is almost perfectly split. About 50.1% said they usually stand on one side and leave the other side open for people in a hurry, while 49.9% said they stand still on both sides.

South Korea has changed its approach several times. In 1998, authorities began encouraging people to stand on one side. This habit spread across the country around 2002, when South Korea co-hosted the soccer World Cup. Then, from 2009 to 2014, the government encouraged people to stand on both sides, because of concerns about accidents and damage to escalators. Since 2015, officials have not told people which side to stand on. Instead, they recommend three safety rules: hold the handrail, do not walk or run, and stay inside the safety lines.
On August 29, about 200 citizens and experts met in Seoul to discuss the issue. After the discussion, 38.1% of participants said the rules should depend on the location and how crowded it is.

Both sides have arguments. An experiment at a busy station in Britain found that escalators carried about 25% to 30% more people when riders stood on both sides. On the other hand, walking on an escalator saves time for each person.

Safety is another issue. Tests found that walking down an escalator creates an impact of about twice a person's body weight. Heo Yun-seop, a professor at Korea Lift College, said this could put stress on escalator parts, though there is not enough evidence that it directly causes breakdowns.
Interior Minister Yun Ho-jung said the government would use the forum's views when planning future escalator safety measures.
